sources.author: smartpostures
sources.text:
1/10 — Band-assisted thoracic extension

This variation uses the bench to support the trunk while the band pulls across the upper arms and the hands stay behind the head.

The useful part is the combination of thoracic extension + shoulder positioning. You’re asking the upper back to extend while the shoulders stay active rather than simply forcing the chest upward.

The common mistake is getting the movement from the lower back instead. Keep the ribs controlled and let the upper back do more of the work.

This can be useful if you spend a lot of time flexed forward, but it isn’t a permanent “posture fix.”

sources.author: postureuni
sources.text:
Your Posture Needs Work‼️

These 5 resistance-band exercises target the muscles that help keep your shoulders and shoulder blades organized:

• Rhomboids + mid/lower traps • Rear delts • Lats • Scapular stabilizers • Upper-back endurance
✔️ Targets The Rhomboids & Mid/Lower Traps To Help Pull Your Shoulders Back
✔️ Strengthens The Rear Delts To Build Better Balance Around The Shoulder Joint
✔️ Activates The Lats & Improves Your Pulling Strength Without Heavy Weights
✔️ Trains The Smaller Stabilizing Muscles That Control Your Shoulder Blades

✔️ Builds Upper-Back Endurance To Help You Maintain Better Posture Throughout The Day

Hours of sitting, driving, and looking down at your phone can leave your chest feeling tight while your upper back does less work than it should.

That’s where these movements come in.

The goal isn't to force your shoulders backward all day.

It’s to build a back strong enough to support better positioning without constant effort.

Keep the reps slow. Control the band. Let the back—not the arms—do the work.

You don't need massive weights.

You need tension, control, and consistency.

sources.author: postureuni
sources.text:
Your shoulders don’t just need to be “strong.”

They need to know how to move, stabilize, and control the shoulder blade under load. 🧠

What caught my attention: the exercises aren’t simply about building bigger back muscles.

They challenge the muscles around the scapula, upper back, rear shoulder, and rotator cuff to work together.

That matters for swimmers, volleyball players, lifters—and anyone spending hours at a desk. 🏊‍♂️🏐🏋️‍♂️

It helps to 
✅ Improve shoulder mobility and stability 
✅ Strengthen the upper and mid-back muscles 
✅ Support better posture and spinal control 
✅ Reduce muscular overload and injury risk

⏱ How to perform: 
• 20-30 seconds per exercise
 • 2-3 sets 
• 2-3 times per week

The goal is having enough strength and control to move well through different positions.

Train the back.
Train the shoulder.
But most importantly: train the connection between them.

sources.author: American Heart Association
sources.text: Warm-up and cool-down guidance.

sources.author: López-Rivera & González-Badillo (2012; 2019)
sources.text: Sport Technology 2012 and J Hum Kinet 2019. 8-week programs: 10 s maximal added-weight hangs, then minimum-edge hangs (MaxHangs), vs intermittent minimum-edge hangs (IntHangs). Grip endurance improved 34% (MaxHangs) and 45% (IntHangs) in advanced climbers.

sources.author: Devise et al. (2022), Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
sources.text: RCT, 54 experienced climbers, 12 mm edge, 2×/week for 4 weeks. 100% max (6 s), 80% (10 s on / 6 s off, up to 12 reps, 3 sets, 8 min rest) and 60% (10 s on / 6 s off, 24 reps, 2 sets, 6 min rest). 100% and 80% raised max strength; 80% and 60% raised endurance.

sources.author: Medernach, Kleinöder & Lötzerich (2015), J Strength Cond Res
sources.text: 4 weeks of fingerboard training in 23 advanced boulderers improved intermittent finger-hang endurance by about 26 s.

sources.author: Levernier & Laffaye (2019), J Strength Cond Res
sources.text: 4 weeks of small-hold hangs, twice a week, raised maximal force and rate of force development in elite boulderers, measured in slope, half-crimp and full-crimp grips.

sources.author: Mundry et al. (2021), Scientific Reports
sources.text: RCT, 8 weeks: hangs with progressively added weight (+1.25 kg/week) improved grip strength vs climbing only; the shorter-hangs endurance group did not differ from control.

sources.author: Gilmore et al. (2024), Sports Medicine – Open
sources.text: Retrospective training-log analysis: frequent low-intensity 10-minute hang sessions (“Abrahangs”) improved finger strength about as much as max hangs; combining both was additive.

sources.author: Stien et al. (2023), Biology of Sport — systematic review & meta-analysis
sources.text: Climbing-specific resistance training and interval bouldering can improve climbing performance; interventional evidence in climbers is still limited.

sources.author: Pull-up contraction regimens RCT (2024), Bioengineering
sources.text: 30 advanced–elite climbers, 5 weeks, 2×/week on a hangboard: eccentric, isometric and plyometric pull-up training all increased max strength; eccentric and plyometric also increased velocity and power.

sources.author: Physical performance testing in climbing — systematic review (2023)
sources.text: Finger strength and pulling capacity (pull-ups, power) discriminate climbing ability; pull-up count correlated strongly with grade in intermediate–advanced climbers.

sources.author: Lattice Training (Climbing magazine)
sources.text: Coaching protocol: 7 s on / 3 s off × 6 = one repeater set, load set so the set is hard but completed; used for strength-endurance.

sources.author: YOGABODY
sources.text: 21-Day Hip Opening Challenge pose chart (Posechart_Hip-Challenge.pdf). Two poses per day with regressions shown on each page.

sources.author: ACSM position stand (Garber et al., 2011)
sources.text: Flexibility: hold stretches 10–30 s to mild tightness, accumulating about 60 s per exercise, on at least 2–3 days per week.

sources.author: McKeon, Hertel, Bramble & Davis (2015), Br J Sports Med
sources.text: The "foot core system": intrinsic foot muscles act as local stabilizers of the arch, parallel to the trunk core. The short-foot exercise is the standard way to isolate and train them.

sources.author: Weight-bearing lunge (knee-to-wall) dorsiflexion test/drill
sources.text: A reliable, widely used measure and mobilization drill for weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion; roughly 3.6 degrees of dorsiflexion per centimetre the knee travels past the toes with the heel down.

sources.author: Baxter, Corrigan, Hullfish et al. (2017), Med Sci Sports Exerc — Achilles tendon loading review
sources.text: Heel-raise and heel-drop exercises progressively and reliably load the Achilles tendon and calf, from an easy seated raise up through single-leg and eccentric variations; the standard rehab progression is double leg to single leg to slow eccentric.

sources.author: DiGiovanni et al. (2006), J Bone Joint Surg — 2-year follow-up RCT
sources.text: A plantar-fascia-specific stretch (pulling the toes back to tension the arch, not just the calf) outperformed a calf-stretch-only protocol for chronic plantar heel pain, with benefits holding at two years.

sources.author: Balance training in chronic ankle instability — systematic review & meta-analysis (2024)
sources.text: Single-leg balance and proprioceptive training improve postural control and self-reported ankle function, and lower re-sprain rates; progressing from eyes-open to eyes-closed increases the demand on the ankle's balance receptors.

Supine wall squat / adductor opener
variants.note: Video label: Olympic wall squat. Post caption: wall adductor opener.

variants.label: Easy walking
variants.note: Walk at an easy pace. For a warm-up, increase gradually; for a cool-down, slow down gradually.

variants.label: Hangboard warm-up hangs
variants.note: Large edge or jugs. Start with feet on a chair taking weight, then build to about 70% effort. Never start a session with max hangs.

variants.label: Max hang · half crimp
variants.note: About 20 mm edge, half crimp, arms straight but shoulders engaged. Add weight (or use a smaller edge) so you could hold ~3 s longer. Rest the full 3 min.

variants.label: Max hang · open hand
variants.note: Open-hand or three-finger drag on a 20 mm edge. Load so ~3 s stays in reserve. Grip strength is grip-specific, so train the positions you climb in.

variants.label: Min-edge hang
variants.note: Bodyweight on the smallest edge you can hold for about 13 s, so 10 s leaves a small reserve. Half crimp. Move to a smaller edge only when it gets easy.

variants.label: Repeaters 7:3
variants.note: 7 s hang, 3 s rest, 6 times = one set. Pick an edge or load where the last reps are hard but you still finish every hang with good form.

variants.label: Intermittent hangs 10:6 · hard
variants.note: Hard, about 80% effort (roughly a load you could hold 20–25 s). 10 s on, 6 s off. End the set early if you cannot finish a hang with good form.

variants.label: Endurance hangs 10:6 · moderate
variants.note: Moderate, about 60% effort: remove weight with a chair or pulley so you can repeat 24 hangs. You should feel a steady pump, not failure.

variants.label: Low-intensity hangs
variants.note: Feet on the floor or a chair so the hang feels easy, well below your max. 10 s on, 20 s off. Gentle enough for most days; skip it if your fingers are sore.

variants.label: Scapular pull-ups
variants.note: From a dead hang with straight arms, pull the shoulder blades down and back to lift the body a few centimetres, then lower slowly.

variants.label: Pull-ups
variants.note: Full range, chin over the bar and fully straight arms at the bottom. Stop 1–2 reps before failure. Use a band or feet on a chair to assist if needed.

variants.label: Weighted pull-ups
variants.note: Add weight (backpack or belt) so 3–5 reps are hard but clean. Rest the full 3 minutes. Without weight, use slower tempo or the hangboard's biggest edge.

variants.label: Explosive pull-ups
variants.note: Pull as fast as possible, aiming the chest toward the bar; lower under control. Stop the set when speed drops. Trains dynamic moves and dynos.

variants.label: Slow negative pull-ups
variants.note: Jump or step to the top, then lower for about 5 s to straight arms. Good for building to more pull-ups or adding eccentric strength.

variants.label: Lock-offs
variants.note: Pull up, then hold about 5 s at the top, 5 s at 90° and 5 s at 120° elbow angle, lowering between positions. Assist with feet if you cannot hold the position.

variants.label: Hanging knee raises
variants.note: Hang with active shoulders and lift the knees toward the chest without swinging. Progress to straight legs or toes-to-bar.

variants.label: Push-up
variants.note: Hands under shoulders, body in one line. Balances the pulling in climbing. Use knees or a wall to make it easier.

variants.label: Pigeon
variants.note: Front shin angled, back leg long. Prop the hip with a block if it floats. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Butterfly
variants.note: Soles together, knees wide. Fold forward only as far as feels easy. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Blaster
variants.note: Low lunge with hands on a chair; sink the hips forward and down. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Passive Squat
variants.note: Deep squat, arms resting forward on a chair or block. Let the hips hang. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Happy Baby
variants.note: On your back, hold the feet and draw the knees toward the armpits. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Thread the Needle (supine)
variants.note: Ankle over opposite knee; pull the lower thigh toward the chest. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Frog
variants.note: Half frog: one knee out to the side at 90°, other leg long. Rest forward on a chair. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Jackknife Blaster
variants.note: Kneeling lunge, back knee padded; reach back for the rear foot if available. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Scissors
variants.note: Staggered stance, hands on a chair or wall; hinge over the straight front leg. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Lightning Bolt
variants.note: Kneel sitting back on the heels; lean back only as far as the knees allow. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Zorro
variants.note: Seated, one shin forward and one leg bent back. Sit tall on a cushion. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Supine Butterfly
variants.note: Soles together, then recline. Use a strap or pillows under the knees. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Thread the Needle @ Wall
variants.note: Seated figure-four: ankle over the opposite knee, walk the hands back. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Prone Butterfly
variants.note: One leg bent in front, the other out behind; lower toward the floor. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Ninja Squats
variants.note: Wide stance, shift into one bent knee with the other leg straight. Use a chair. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Lateral Chain Stretch
variants.note: Side-lying on a forearm, legs stacked; lift the hip gently to lengthen the side. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Psoas Blaster (chair)
variants.note: Back knee on a padded chair, front foot forward; press the hips forward. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Reclined Scissors
variants.note: On your back with one leg up on a chair or wall; keep the other leg long. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Blaster Twist
variants.note: Low lunge, rotate the chest toward the front knee. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Squat Twist
variants.note: Deep squat, elbow inside one knee, rotate open. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Double Pigeon
variants.note: Stack the shins. Sit on a block or chair; fold forward gently. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Bound Butterfly
variants.note: Butterfly with a forward fold; rest the arms on a chair or block. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Eagle Fold
variants.note: Cross one thigh over the other, then fold forward over the legs. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Cross-Thread
variants.note: On your back, cross the thighs and hug the legs toward the chest. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Swiss Army Knife
variants.note: Kneeling lunge; loop a strap around the back foot and draw it up. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Saddle
variants.note: From kneeling on the heels, lean back onto the hands or forearms. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Butterfly Squat
variants.note: Deep squat with knees wide; hold a chair or pole for balance. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Half Lightning Bolt
variants.note: One leg folded back, the other long. Lean back only as far as comfortable. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Fallen Blaster
variants.note: Long low lunge, back knee down; support the chest on a chair. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: A-Baby
variants.note: On your back, hold one straight leg up; keep the other leg long. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Standing Psoas
variants.note: Back shin on a table or bench, front leg standing; tuck the pelvis. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Standing Pigeon
variants.note: Front shin across a table, hinge forward from the hips. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Sage Fold
variants.note: Seated, one leg long and one bent; reach forward along the long leg. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Long Butterfly
variants.note: Soles together with feet further away; fold forward and relax the back. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Eagle Legs
variants.note: Seated, cross one leg over the other and hug the shin toward you. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Chair Squat
variants.note: Standing figure-four holding a chair: ankle on the opposite knee, sit back. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Twisted Pigeon
variants.note: From pigeon, rotate the chest toward the back leg. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Bound Baby
variants.note: On your back, hold both feet with the knees wide and drawn down. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Seated Pigeon
variants.note: On a chair, ankle over the opposite knee; hinge forward with a long spine. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Railroad Squat
variants.note: Deep squat holding a pole or doorframe; keep the heels down if you can. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Thunderbolt
variants.note: Kneel sitting on the heels; add a cushion under the seat if needed. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Prayer Squat
variants.note: Deep squat, palms together, elbows gently pressing the knees wide. Props shown are optional.

variants.label: Ankle circles
variants.note: Lift one foot and slowly circle the ankle, 30 s each direction, then switch feet. Go slowly and make the circle as big as you can without moving the shin. Tracing the alphabet with your big toe works the same way.

variants.label: Knee-to-wall ankle mobilization
variants.note: Half-kneel facing a wall, front foot a few inches back. Keeping the heel down, drive the knee forward over the toes toward the wall and back, 10 slow reps, then switch feet. Move the foot back as it gets easy.

variants.label: Short foot hold
variants.note: Barefoot, stand or sit with toes flat and relaxed. Without curling the toes, draw the ball of the foot toward the heel to gently dome the arch. Hold 10 s, relax, repeat. This is the classic "foot core" exercise for the intrinsic foot muscles.

variants.label: Toe splay & lift
variants.note: Spread the toes apart as wide as you can, then lift just the big toe while the other four stay down, then reverse: lift the four small toes while the big toe stays down. Slow and controlled — the separation is the hard part.

variants.label: Toe spread & squeeze
variants.note: Spread all ten toes as wide apart as possible and hold for 2–3 s, then relax and let them come back together. A folded towel or toe spacer between the toes makes this easier to feel at first.

variants.label: Towel curls
variants.note: Lay a towel flat on the floor under one foot. Scrunch it toward you using only your toes, then reset and repeat. Add a light weight on the far end of the towel to make it harder.

variants.label: Marble pickups
variants.note: Pick up small objects (marbles, a scrunched sock, pebbles) one at a time with your toes and place them in a cup. Keeps the toe flexors and arch working through a full range.

variants.label: Double-leg heel raises
variants.note: Rise onto the balls of both feet as high as you can, then lower slowly over about 3 s. Hold a wall or chair for balance if needed. The easiest, lowest-load way to build calf and Achilles capacity.

variants.label: Single-leg heel raises
variants.note: Standing on one foot (fingertips on a wall for balance), rise onto the ball of the foot and lower slowly. Roughly double the load of a two-footed raise — progress here once double raises feel easy.

variants.label: Bent-knee heel raises
variants.note: Soften the knees into a slight bend and hold it while you raise and lower onto the balls of the feet. Bending the knee takes the gastrocnemius out and shifts the load onto the soleus, deeper in the calf.

variants.label: Heel raises · toes elevated
variants.note: Rest the balls of your feet on a rolled towel or a low step so the toes sit higher than the heels, then raise and lower. The extra toe extension adds plantar-fascia and arch loading to the calf work.

variants.label: Tibialis raises
variants.note: Lean your back against a wall, feet a little out in front, and lift the toes and forefoot up off the floor as high as you can, then lower slowly. Trains the tibialis anterior, the dorsiflexor that balances all the calf-raise work.

variants.label: Ankle eversion & inversion with band
variants.note: Loop a band around the forefoot and anchor it to the side. Turn the foot outward (away from the band) for the reps, then turn the foot inward against the band, then switch feet. Trains the muscles that resist rolling an ankle.

variants.label: Toe & heel walks in place
variants.note: March in place on your tiptoes for 20 s, then flip to walking on your heels with the toes lifted for 20 s. Builds calf and shin endurance through the ranges you actually walk in.

variants.label: Single-leg balance
variants.note: Stand on one foot, eyes open, soft knee, and hold as still as you can. Keep a fingertip near a wall the first few times. Try looking around or tapping the free foot lightly to the floor and back to add challenge.

variants.label: Single-leg balance · eyes closed
variants.note: Stand on one foot and close your eyes once you feel steady. Removing vision forces the small muscles of the foot and ankle to do the balancing. Open your eyes any time you feel unsteady, then reset.

variants.label: Foot rolling on a ball
variants.note: Stand or sit and roll the arch of one foot slowly over a ball (a lacrosse or tennis ball works) for 45 s, easing off any tender spot rather than grinding into it, then switch feet.

variants.label: Calf stretch · straight knee
variants.note: Hands on a wall, back leg straight with the heel down, front knee bent. Lean the hips forward until you feel a stretch up the back of the straight leg's calf. Hold, then switch legs.

variants.label: Calf stretch · bent knee
variants.note: Same wall lean, but bend both knees, keeping the back heel down. Bending the back knee shifts the stretch lower, into the soleus. Hold, then switch legs.

variants.label: Plantar fascia stretch
variants.note: Sit and cross one foot over the opposite knee. Pull the toes back toward the shin with your hand until you feel a stretch along the arch, not just the calf. Hold, then switch feet.
